newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Ekeus to seek Iraqi explanation on missing arms.
newsitem.headline: Ekeus to seek Iraqi explanation on missing arms.

text.p: Chief U.N. weapons inspector Rolf Ekeus said on Friday he would hold talks with Iraqi officials to seek an explanation on prohibited arms which are unaccounted for.
"This visit is an arrangement we made in June between myself and (Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister) Tariq Aziz," Ekeus told reporters in Bahrain.
"We should jointly assess developments in the last three months, outline and give directives to the work in the coming period. We see this an important routine type of visit," he said.
Ekeus on Friday arrived in Bahrain, field headquarters of U.N. missions visiting Baghdad to eliminate Iraq's weapons of mass destruction in accordance with the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire.
He is due to travel to Baghdad on Saturday.
"Iraq admits that its has (arms) not accounted for...but they said these items were destroyed unilaterally and in that sense they were accounted for.
"Our programme is now to verify that the destruction indeed took place," Ekeus said.
Asked how many missiles he suspected Iraq might be hiding, Ekeus replied: "I said (between) six to 16. We are trying to narrow the numbers now."
"We told the Security Council that we felt the dialogue on the political level has been fruitful...So we welcome that dialogue and we hope for tangible results," Ekeus said.

Iraq is fighting to lift or ease crippling U.N. sanctions imposed after its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait. Elimination of weapons of mass destruction is a prerequisite to the lifting of the sanctions.
Ekeus said on Thursday it would be a "major achievement" if Iraq accounted for a number of missiles capable of carrying biological or chemical warfare agents.
"It is a real matter of life and death for the states in the region, and therefore we cannot rest until we have accounted for them," he added.

Iraq gave Ekeus' deputy Charles Duelfer, who was in Baghdad this month, nine letters attempting to clarify its disclosure of banned weapons after the U.N. official told the press Iraq's original declarations were flawed and incomplete.
Ekeus said in Bahrain 48 Iraqi missiles were handed over and destroyed under U.N. supervision after the Gulf War.
